Orthopedics · published research

Tennis elbow

Some sham-controlled trials report short-term pain and grip improvement with selected low-level laser protocols; other trials found no advantage over sham. A 2025 PBM-plus-static-field trial improved pain response but not elbow function or grip, so the light component cannot be isolated.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Some sham-controlled trials report short-term pain and grip improvement with selected low-level laser protocols; other trials found no advantage over sham. A 2025 PBM-plus-static-field trial improved pain response but not elbow function or grip, so the light component cannot be isolated.

Summary of the Evidence

The exact Tendons > Tennis elbow category contains 38 unique titles. One title appears misclassified: a randomized carpal-tunnel study is not direct tennis-elbow evidence, leaving 37 relevant publications. These include 28 human clinical reports, seven review or meta-analysis publications, and two letters. Reviews synthesize primary trials and do not add cohorts. Three Haker and Lundeberg reports appear to describe the same 49-person cohort, and two Vasseljen reports appear to share 30 participants. The 1998 multicentre study included both medial and lateral epicondylitis, so the records do not represent 37 independent cohorts.

Human and clinical evidence

Clinical findings vary with wavelength, delivery site, dose, comparator, and whether exercise or another treatment is combined. In a 39-person sham-controlled trial, 904-nm laser added to exercise improved pain threshold, grip-related pain, grip strength, and most DASH outcomes over nine sessions (Lam and Cheing 2007). Several sham-controlled trials were null. A 52-person Nd:YAG trial found the tested protocol safe but ineffective, and another placebo-controlled trial found no added short-term benefit (Basford et al. 2000 Emanet et al. 2010).

An 18-trial review identified 13 trials with 730 participants for meta-analysis. Its subgroup analyses found short-term pain and disability improvement when selected 904-nm, and possibly 632-nm, protocols directly irradiated tendon insertions; trials using other wavelengths or acupuncture-point targeting did not show the same pattern (Bjordal et al. 2008). A later meta-analysis of 12 randomized trials reported improvements across low- and high-intensity laser studies, but mixed protocols and comparisons limit what can be concluded for one PBM regimen (Zhang et al. 2026).

A 50-person sham-controlled trial reported more pain responders with PBM plus a static magnetic field than with sham, 72% versus 40%, but did not find corresponding improvement in forearm function or grip strength. Because the device combined light and a magnetic field, it does not isolate PBM (de Oliveira et al. 2025).

Animal evidence

No animal evidence was identified in the exact tennis-elbow category.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No standalone in-vitro or ex-vivo evidence was identified in the exact category.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The database includes visible red and near-infrared laser protocols, including 904-nm treatment at 0.275 J per tender point for nine sessions and other 904-nm protocols using about 2.4 J/cm². Older reports also used 633, 830, or 1060 nm. High-intensity protocols used substantially different outputs, while the 2025 combined-device trial used 640-, 850-, and 905-nm light with a static magnetic field over six sessions in three weeks. Power, fluence, irradiation time, treatment points, exercise, and follow-up were not reported consistently. High-intensity treatment, broad-spectrum polarized light, and PBM with a magnetic field are not interchangeable. No direct dose-finding comparison establishes an optimal protocol.

Interpretation

Selected low-level laser protocols have shown short-term pain benefits, but null trials, mixed modalities, overlapping publications, and uncertain long-term functional results keep confidence low. The evidence does not establish durable recovery or modification of tendon disease.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow for short-term pain relief with specific low-level laser protocols Very low for durable functional recovery and disease modification
Publications and records37 relevant titles from 38 exact-category records; one carpal-tunnel RCT appears misclassified.

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

The evidence includes multiple randomized trials and a meta-analysis with a favorable dose-specific subgroup, but results differ across wavelengths and several blinded studies were null. Some apparent replication comes from overlapping reports, and recent positive pain findings used PBM combined with a static magnetic field. Larger independent sham-controlled trials should isolate light, standardize tendon targeting and dose, and assess daily function through longer follow-up.
